newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy parlt backs Albania force, Prodi faces test.
newsitem.headline: Italy parlt backs Albania force, Prodi faces test.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi won support on Wednesday to send an Italian-led security force to Albania but at the cost of a rift with his hard left allies that will expose his government to a confidence test in parliament.
The Chamber of Deputies (lower house) voted by an overwhelming 503 to 85 with seven abstentions to deploy the multinational force, the first of its kind to be led by Italy.

Prodi needed the backing of the main centre-right opposition Freedom Alliance to secure the victory on a joint resolution after a key parliamentary ally, the Communist Refoundation party, deserted him on the issue and voted 'no'.

The mutiny, Prodi's stiffest political challenge in 11 months in office, means he must now submit to confidence votes in both houses of parliament that will decide whether his centre-left government stands or falls.
Prodi was told to face the test by President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro, whom he met after the Albania vote to discuss Refoundation's stance, a presidential office statement said.
Political sources said the Senate, where Prodi's coalition has a majority in its own right, was expected to hold its vote late on Thursday.
The Chamber, where the government cannot survive without the support of Refoundation's 34 deputies, must also vote though the timing was unclear.

Refoundation has signalled it will back the government but coalition parties now want a thorough review of the alliance to determine whether the party can be brought into line on key economic policies.
Prodi staved off an immediate government crisis when the centre-right opposition said it would support a joint motion on the Albania force, whose deployment is expected next week.
But it exacted a high price for voting with the government, forcing Prodi into a humiliating admission that he was not able to muster a majority of his own.
Freedom Alliance leader Silvio Berlusconi said opposition votes had saved Italy from becoming "the laughing stock of Europe and the world" and urged Prodi to dump his Marxist ally.
He said his opposition bloc would consider lending support in parliament to a minority government. "Take a decision...we are ready to make our contribution," he told the debate.

The split on Albania has highlighted the vulnerability of his coalition to Refoundation's casting votes on a difficult domestic agenda, including a drive to reform the welfare state to prepare Italy for Europe's planned single currency.

"What we have to do now is seek a confidence vote on the government's programme. The vote must be on precise issues and not general matters," said Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini, leader of the centrist Italian Renewal party.
Refoundation has said it will back Prodi on a confidence vote but party chairman Armando Cossutta appeared on Wednesday to lay down terms, signalling a potentially rocky ride ahead.

"If Prodi wants (to win) the confidence motion, then he should not enter into details," Cossutta told reporters. "If we back the motion then we will vote for it with open hearts. If not then we will vote against," he added.

Refoundation regards the Albania force as a neo-colonialist venture and says Italian soldiers will face unacceptable risks. The mission coincides with the 58th anniversary this week of the occupation of the country by pre-war Fascist Italy.
